title: Episode 184: Lyndon B. Johnson: The Great Society, Civil Rights, and the Beagles (1963–1969)
description:
Five days after John F. Kennedy's assassination, President Lyndon B. Johnson addressed a joint session of Congress and issued a commanding challenge: 'Let us continue.' Wielding his unparalleled legislative mastery and invoking the memory of the martyred president, Johnson shattered a fifty-four-day southern filibuster to sign the epochal Civil Rights Act of 1964, outlawing racial segregation across America. In 1964, he won the presidency in a historic landslide behind the controversial 'Daisy' television commercial, then launched the 'Great Society'—enacting Medicare, Medicaid, Head Start, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Yet alongside these monumental triumphs were colorful White House spectacles, including lifting his beloved beagles 'Him' and 'Her' by their ears for photographers. Discover the monumental triumphs and tragic undoing of Lyndon B. Johnson.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our Lyndon B. Johnson saga with the high drama of the Great Society. In five breathless years, LBJ transformed American law and conquered poverty, all while delighting and confounding the public with his irrepressible Texas flair. But the shadows of Vietnam would claim his presidency. Here is George with the story of the Civil Rights Act, the White House beagles, and the tragic fall of a giant.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: 'LET US CONTINUE': THE CIVIL RIGHTS ACT OF 1964
On November 27, 1963, five days after Kennedy's assassination, Lyndon Johnson strode into the House chamber to address a grief-stricken nation. When cautious political advisors begged him not to waste his political capital on civil rights, warning that southern senators would filibuster and destroy his presidency, Johnson gave an answer that defined his moral greatness: 'Well, what the hell is the presidency for?' Johnson transformed national sorrow into irresistible legislative momentum. For fifty-four grueling days in the summer of 1964, southern senators mounted the longest filibuster in Senate history to block the Civil Rights Bill. Johnson went to work with demonic energy, applying the Johnson Treatment to wavering Republicans, courted Senate Minority Leader Everett Dirksen, and secured the votes to break the filibuster. On July 2, 1964, Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, using seventy-two ceremonial pens to outlaw racial segregation in all public accommodations, end discrimination in employment, and dismantle the evil edifice of Jim Crow. Handing the first pen to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Johnson knew the political cost, privately confessing to aide Bill Moyers: 'I think we just delivered the South to the Republican Party for a long time to come.' In seizing the tragic moment to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Johnson proved that true political greatness requires risking one's own partisan advantage to right a historic national injustice. In passing the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Johnson fulfilled the promise of the Emancipation Proclamation, dismantling legal segregation forever.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE WHITE HOUSE BEAGLES: HIM AND HER
Despite his volcanic legislative power, Lyndon Johnson was a country boy at heart who loved dogs with unabashed passion. Living with him in the White House was a famous pair of tri-colored beagles named 'Him' and 'Her,' who routinely slept on the foot of the presidential bed, rode in the presidential limousine, and barked joyously around the South Lawn. In April 1964, an innocent photo opportunity erupted into a nationwide comic controversy. Walking the dogs on the South Lawn before a crowd of tourists and White House photographers, Johnson bent down, gently lifted Him by the loose skin of his ears until the beagle let out a loud yelp. When reporters gasped in shock, Johnson grinned broadly and explained with folksy Texas nonchalance: 'Why, it does them good to let them yelp! It's good for them! It helps them bark!' The next morning, newspapers across America were plastered with front-page photographs of the President pulling his dog's ears, igniting a humorous firestorm of angry letters from dog lovers and humane societies. Johnson chuckled at the uproar, inviting the press to watch the beagles lick his face to prove their undying mutual affection. The nationwide uproar over pulling his beagles' ears revealed the immense public fascination with every detail of the presidential family, humanizing the volcanic Texas giant in the eyes of ordinary citizens. The humorous incident with the beagles showed a president who was entirely comfortable in his own skin, unbothered by the delicate sensibilities of Washington critics.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE 1964 LANDSLIDE AND THE DAISY AD
In the autumn of 1964, Johnson ran for a full presidential term against conservative Republican champion Senator Barry Goldwater of Arizona. Goldwater's aggressive rhetoric regarding the potential use of tactical nuclear weapons in Vietnam provided Johnson's campaign with the opportunity to create the most famous and devastating political television commercial in history: the 'Daisy Ad.' Aired only once on September 7, 1964, the black-and-white commercial showed a three-year-old girl plucking petals from a daisy, counting unevenly. As she reached ten, the camera zoomed into her pupil, replaced by a booming military countdown, culminating in a colossal nuclear mushroom cloud, over which Johnson's resonant Texas voice proclaimed: 'These are the stakes: to make a world in which all of God's children can live, or go into the dark. We must either love each other, or we must die.' The ad terrified the electorate. In November 1964, Johnson won forty-three million votes to Goldwater's twenty-seven million—a sixty-one point one percent popular vote mandate that remains the highest share of the popular vote in modern American history. The crushing landslide of 1964 provided Johnson with an unprecedented congressional majority that enabled him to enact the most sweeping domestic welfare legislation since the New Deal. The 1964 landslide demonstrated the overwhelming national consensus behind Johnson's vision of a compassionate, prosperous, and fair society.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: SELMA AND 'WE SHALL OVERCOME': 1965
Armed with his colossal electoral mandate, Johnson launched the 'Great Society'—an ambitious, sweeping domestic crusade to eradicate poverty and racial injustice. But in March 1965, violence erupted in Selma, Alabama, when state troopers brutally attacked peaceful civil rights marchers with clubs and tear gas on the Edmund Pettus Bridge on 'Bloody Sunday.' Eight days later, Johnson seized the moral conscience of the nation. Standing before a joint session of Congress and seventy million television viewers, Johnson delivered what many consider the finest presidential speech on civil rights in American history: 'Their cause must be our cause too. Because it is not just Negroes, but really it is all of us, who must overcome the crippling legacy of bigotry and injustice.' Then, looking directly into the cameras, Johnson raised his arm and spoke the sacred anthem of the civil rights movement: 'And we shall overcome.' In Atlanta, watching television beside his associates, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. wept open tears of joy. In August 1965, Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act, deploying federal registrars to guarantee the sacred right to vote for millions of African Americans. When Lyndon Johnson looked into the cameras and uttered 'And we shall overcome,' he forged a historic alliance between the power of the federal government and the moral crusade of the civil rights movement. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 tore down the final barriers to political participation, bringing millions of disenfranchised citizens into the heart of American democracy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GREAT SOCIETY AVALANCHE: MEDICARE AND BEYOND
Between 1965 and 1968, Johnson pushed an astonishing two hundred major legislative programs through Congress—an avalanche unmatched since FDR's New Deal. Flying to Independence, Missouri, in July 1965, Johnson sat beside eighty-one-year-old Harry S. Truman to sign the historic Medicare Act, guaranteeing healthcare for elderly Americans, presenting Truman with the very first Medicare card. In rapid succession, Johnson created Medicaid for low-income citizens, Head Start for underprivileged preschool children, the Elementary and Secondary Education Act to fund public schools, the National Endowment for the Arts and Humanities, the Department of Housing and Urban Development (appointing Robert C. Weaver as the first African American cabinet secretary), and the Public Broadcasting Act, which created PBS and Sesame Street. In his private moments, Johnson loved conducting business while surrounded by aides, famously summoning cabinet members into the bathroom to dictate policy from the toilet, delighting in shocking the Washington establishment with his complete lack of pretension. The passage of Medicare and Medicaid fundamentally reshaped the American social contract, guaranteeing dignity and medical care to tens of millions of elderly and low-income citizens. The legislative deluge of the Great Society built the modern American safety net, lifting millions of families out of poverty and providing dignity to the elderly.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE AGONY AND QUAGMIRE OF VIETNAM
Yet even as the Great Society transformed American life, the tragic quagmire of the Vietnam War was steadily swallowing Lyndon Johnson's presidency whole. Haunted by the fear that communist expansion in Southeast Asia would trigger World War III or provoke a right-wing backlash that would destroy his domestic reforms, Johnson escalated the war step by agonizing step. In August 1964, following the disputed Gulf of Tonkin incident, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, handing Johnson a blank check to wage war without a formal declaration. By 1968, Johnson had committed five hundred and forty-nine thousand American troops to the jungles of Vietnam. Over thirty thousand young Americans had returned home in flag-draped coffins. When the communist forces launched the massive Tet Offensive in January 1968, striking sixty-four cities across South Vietnam, the illusion that the war was being won shattered entirely. Respected CBS news anchor Walter Cronkite declared the war an unwinnable stalemate, prompting Johnson to whisper in despair: 'If I've lost Cronkite, I've lost Middle America.' Anti-war protesters besieged the White House, chanting through the night: 'Hey, hey, LBJ, how many kids did you kill today?' The agonizing escalation of the Vietnam War became an inescapable trap that broke Johnson's heart, tearing apart the national consensus and overshadowing his extraordinary domestic triumphs. The tragic quagmire of Vietnam revealed the painful limits of military power, consuming the energies of a president who dreamed only of conquering human misery at home.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: 'I SHALL NOT SEEK, AND I WILL NOT ACCEPT'
On Sunday evening, March 31, 1968, an exhausted, haggard Lyndon Johnson sat before television cameras in the Oval Office to announce a unilateral bombing halt over North Vietnam and offer peace negotiations. Then, looking into the lens with deep solemnity, Johnson uttered words that stunned the world: 'I have concluded that I should not permit the presidency to become involved in the partisan divisions that are developing in this political year... Accordingly, I shall not seek, and I will not accept, the nomination of my party for another term as your President.' Walking away from supreme power voluntarily, Johnson spent his remaining ten months in office seeking peace. He retired to his beloved Texas ranch, grew his hair long over his collar in the style of the young generation, walked his dogs along the river, and established his presidential library in Austin. On January 22, 1973—just days before the Paris Peace Accords were signed ending American involvement in Vietnam—Lyndon B. Johnson suffered a fatal heart attack at the age of sixty-four. He remains a tragic, gargantuan figure: a flawed giant who lifted millions out of poverty and bondage, yet was ultimately consumed by the fires of an intractable war. His stunning decision to walk away from the presidency in 1968 stands as an unforgettable act of political sacrifice, stepping aside in the desperate hope of restoring unity to a deeply divided nation. His voluntary departure from power stands as a monument to his patriotism, prioritizing the healing of a wounded nation above his own political survival.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Lyndon B. Johnson's gargantuan presidency reshaped the American landscape, leaving behind a legacy of transformative civil rights triumphs and agonizing foreign tragedy. Following his departure, the nation turned to a figure who had spent eight years in the political wilderness: Richard Milhous Nixon. Next week, we turn to the dramatic rise and fall of Richard Nixon: the Checkers Speech, the opening to China, the secret Oval Office taping system, and the Watergate scandal that forced a sitting president to resign. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
